t.6.1: His sharp arrows the shoots of blossoming mango, his bowstring a gleaming line of bees, Spring the warrior has come, my beloved, to pierce the hearts of those devoted to love's delights.
t.6.2: Trees are laden with blossoms, the waters bear lotuses, women are full of desire, and the breeze is fragrant; the evenings are pleasant and the days delightful. In spring, beloved, everything is more lovely.
t.6.4: This spring bestows beauty and charm upon the waters of the step-wells, upon jeweled girdles, upon the radiance of the moon, upon young women, and upon mango trees laden with blossoms.
t.6.3: With the mansions made cool by a light spray of mist, women too, in springtime, make their lovely heads fragrant with campaka blossoms and adorn their breasts with garlands of enchanting flowers.
t.6.5: The rounded hips of graceful women are adorned with silken garments reddened with safflower dye, and their full breasts with delicate cloths made golden by the hue of saffron.
t.6.7: Necklaces moist with white sandal paste come to rest upon the breasts, bracelets and armlets upon the arms, and girdles upon the hips of full-hipped women whose minds are tormented by Anaṅga.
t.6.6: Fresh karṇikāra blossoms fit for the ears, aśoka flowers set in dark, restless curls, and the full-blown blossom of the navamallikā all come to share in the loveliness of young women.
t.6.8: On the faces of playful women, adorned with painted leaf-designs and resembling golden lotuses, the welling of sweat, lovely as though strung with pearls, spreads wide amid their jewels.
t.6.9: Letting their limbs breathe free, their fastenings loosened and their bodies overwhelmed by Kandarpa, women now grow truly eager for their beloveds who are close at hand.
t.6.10: Anaṅga makes the limbs of young women slender and pale, languid with passion, given again and again to yawning, and stirred with restless loveliness.
t.6.11: People long for the shade of trees, and at night they desire again the rays of the nectar-rayed moon; they go up to the mansion roof to sleep where it is pleasant and cool, and they clasp their beloved tightly for her coolness.
t.6.12: Today Anaṅga dwells in women's bodies in many forms: restless in their eyes languid with wine, pale in their cheeks, firm in their breasts, deep in their waists, and full in their hips.
t.6.14: Sandal paste, blended with priyaṅgu, kālīyaka and saffron and mixed with musk, is smeared upon their fair breasts by playful women, languid with the intoxication of passion.
t.6.13: Kāma made the limbs of lovely women sway with the languor of sleep, their words a little drowsy with wine, and their glances sidelong with the arching of their brows.
t.6.15: Swiftly casting off their heavy garments, people whose limbs are languid with the intoxication of love put on thin ones, dyed with lac-juice and perfumed with the smoke of fragrant black aloe-wood.
t.6.16: The male cuckoo, drunk on the wine of mango juice and thrilled with passion, kisses his beloved; and this humming bee too, resting in a lotus, whispers sweet flatteries to his beloved.
t.6.17: The mango trees, bowed low with clusters of copper-red shoots, their lovely branches in blossom and shaken by the wind, awaken desire and make the hearts of women restless with longing.
t.6.18: The aśoka trees, with their fresh shoots, bearing masses of blossoms copper-red as coral from the very base, fill the hearts of young women in the bloom of youth with sorrow as they gaze upon them.
t.6.20: Beloved, having seen the supreme beauty of the newly risen blossom-clusters of the kurabaka trees, which share the radiance of a lovely woman's face, whose heart, if he is a man of feeling, would not be pained by the falling of Kandarpa's arrows?
t.6.19: The young atimukta creepers, their lovely flowers kissed by intoxicated bees and their soft, drooping shoots stirred by the gentle breeze, suddenly awaken longing in the hearts of lovers as they gaze upon them.
t.6.21: Covered all at once by the season of spring with kiṃśuka groves everywhere, resembling a blazing fire, shaken by the wind and bowed down with blossoms, this earth shines like a new bride in a red garment.
t.6.22: What has not been pierced by the kiṃśuka blossoms, glowing like a parrot's beak? What, indeed, has not been burned by the karṇikāra flowers, that this cuckoo now, once more, with its sweet calls, strikes down the hearts of young men already given to fair-faced women?
t.6.23: By the male cuckoos, joyful and sweet of voice, and by the bees humming notes sweet with intoxication, the modest and well-mannered hearts of young wives are in a moment thrown into turmoil, even within their family homes.
t.6.24: Shaking the blossoming branches of the mango trees and spreading the cuckoo's calls in every direction, the wind blows in spring, stealing the hearts of men, delightful now that the falling of frost has passed.
t.6.25: The charming groves, lit up by jasmine blossoms as white as the laughter of flirtatious young women, steal away the mind even of a sage who has renounced passion, so how much more the hearts of young men already stained with desire.
t.6.28: The traveler, his mind worn out by separation from his beloved, on seeing the mango trees in bloom, closes his eyes, weeps, falls into grief, covers his nose with his hand, and cries out aloud.
t.6.26: In the month of Madhu, the dangling golden girdles of a woman, the necklaces clinging to her breasts, and her slender limbs made languid by the pride of Kandarpa, together with the sweet calls of cuckoos and the humming of bees, forcibly steal away the hearts of men.
t.6.27: Seeing those mountains adorned with trees bearing many kinds of lovely blossoms, their slopes filled with the cries of joyful cuckoos, and their stretches of rock overspread with webs of moss, all people are filled with delight.
t.6.29: Delightful with the humming of maddened bees and the calls of cuckoos, with mango trees in bloom and with karṇikāra flowers, the month of blossoms pierces the hearts of proud women as if with very sharp arrows, to kindle the fire of Manmatha.
t.6.30: Seeing before him on the road the blossoming mango trees, shaken by the gentle breeze and shedding heaps of flowers that gleam with the lovely lustre of gold, the traveller far from home, though his body is already wasted, swoons under the blows of Madana's arrows.
t.6.31: Now spring mocks the sweet words of lovely women with the delightful soft songs of the cuckoos, the gleam of their smiling teeth with the radiance of kunda blossoms, and the beauty of their bud-like hands with young leaves glowing like coral.
t.6.32: With faces lovely as golden lotuses, with pale cheeks, with the swell of their breasts moist with sandal paste and hung with necklaces, and with glances full of the playful charm born of passion, women bowed by the weight of their breasts stir desire even in the foremost of sages, though their minds are wholly at peace.
t.6.33: The lotus face fragrant with honey-wine, the eyes coppery like lodhra blossoms, the charming mass of hair filled with fresh kurabaka flowers, the heavy pair of breasts and the round orb of the hips as well: what of women does not now serve Manmatha?
t.6.34: The hearts of proud women are set trembling by breezes perfumed by the full-blossomed mango trees, by the high-pitched calls of the cuckoo frenzied with passion, and by the humming songs of the bee, so pleasing to the ear.
t.6.35: The lovely hour of evening, the bright light of the moon, the call of the male cuckoo, the fragrant breeze, the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees, and the drinking of sīdhu at night: all this is an elixir for Kusumāyudha.
t.6.36: May the Coming of Flowers, beloved of Madana, the guru who initiates into love, grant you blessings until the end of the kalpa: Spring, whose sweet lower lip is fashioned of red aśoka, whose voice is the hum of intoxicated bees, whose row of pure white teeth is a garland of kunda blossoms, whose face is the full-blown lotus, and whose gentle breeze is fragrant with the scent of mango blossoms.
t.6.37: Pierced by the breeze from Malaya, delightful with the calls of cuckoos, having gained an unbroken stream of fragrance from the sprinkling of sweet-scented honey, and encircled on all sides by swarms of many kinds of bees, may spring, the finest of seasons, bring you happiness.
t.6.38: He whose choice arrow is the mango with its lovely cluster of blossoms, whose bow is the splendid kiṃśuka, whose bowstring is a swarm of bees, whose spotless white parasol is the moon, whose rutting elephant is the Malaya breeze, and whose bards are the cuckoos: may this Bodiless One, conqueror of the worlds, accompanied by Spring, lavishly bestow good fortune upon you.
